procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 06.04.2023 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad in A482 No.38114 of 2022, titled ‘Jitendra Mishra @ Sanjay and Ors. Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh and Anr.’ (the “Impugned Order”). This order accepted an application under Section 482 CrPC and set aside the proceedings of the case.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. Accused Persons preferred (i) a criminal revision petition assailing inter alia the Summoning Order (the “Revision Petition”); and (ii) an application under Section 482 CrPC seeking the quashing of the Chargesheet before the High Court (the “Quashing Petition”). Vide an order dated 28.05.2010, the High Court dismissed both (i) the Revision Petition; and (ii) the Quashing Petition (the “1st HC Order”).
2. Accused Persons brought a settlement agreement dated 28.09.2022 to the notice of the Trial Court and filed an application under Section 482 CrPC before the High Court seeking quashing of the proceedings emanating from the FIR on the basis of the Settlement Agreement (the “1st Settlement Application”).
3. Vide an order dated 23.12.2022 in the 1st Settlement Application, the High Court directed the Trial Court to consider the Settlement Agreement and pass appropriate order(s) within a period of 1 (one) month (the “2nd HC Order”).
4. The High Court passed the Impugned Order on 06.04.2023, accepting an application under Section 482 CrPC and setting aside the proceedings of the case.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellant, the original complainant and injured victim, appealed the High Court's Impugned Order, arguing that the High Court erred in allowing the 2nd Settlement Application because the Appellant was not a party to it and the order suffers from perversity and illegality.

directions: The Impugned Order is set aside.
The proceedings emanating from FIR i.e., Case No. 1288 of 2003, stand restored to the file of the Trial Court.
The Trial Court is directed to dispose of the same expeditiously, preferably, within a period of one year.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the entire proceedings of the case against the accused on the basis of a Settlement Agreement where the complainant in the FIR was not made a party.

facts: An FIR was filed by the Appellant, who was also an injured victim in the case.
The accused persons entered into a Settlement Agreement with another victim (Respondent No. 5), but not with the Appellant.

The Trial Court rejected this agreement, noting that some offenses were non-compoundable and, crucially, that the original complainant (the Appellant) was not a party to the settlement and had objected to it.
The accused persons then approached the High Court, which, exercising its power under Section 482 CrPC, quashed the entire criminal proceedings based on this settlement.
law: The Supreme Court referred to the principles established in the case of Gian Singh v. State of Punjab.
According to this precedent, a High Court can use its inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC to quash criminal proceedings based on a settlement between the victim and the wrongdoer.

However, this power should only be exercised to secure the ends of justice or to prevent an abuse of the legal process. The court must consider if it would be unfair or contrary to justice to continue the proceedings after a genuine compromise.
application: The Supreme Court applied the principles of Gian Singh to the facts of the case.
It noted that the Appellant was undisputedly the original complainant and an injured victim.
The Court found it critical that the Appellant was never a party to the Settlement Agreement and was not agreeable to quashing the proceedings.
The High Court completely failed to consider this essential fact.

By quashing the proceedings without the consent or involvement of the primary complainant and victim, the High Court's order did not secure the ends of justice. Instead, it was contrary to the principles laid down in Gian Singh.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had erred and was not justified in setting aside the criminal proceedings. The decision was based on a flawed settlement agreement that excluded the original complainant and injured victim, which meant that quashing the case did not secure the ends of justice.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the entire proceedings of the case against the accused on the basis of a Settlement Agreement where the complainant in the FIR was not made a party.
appellant_arguments: The appellant is the original complainant and an injured victim of the alleged offence.
The High Court erred by allowing the settlement application and quashing the proceedings because the appellant was not a party to the Settlement Agreement.
The High Court should not have exercised its jurisdiction under Section 482 CrPC in favour of the accused persons as the original complainant had not settled the matter.
respondent_arguments: The accused persons entered into a settlement with the principal victim who was allegedly abducted (Respondent No. 5).
Once the principal victim had settled the matter, there was no justifiable reason to continue the criminal proceedings against the accused.
The High Court's order quashing the proceedings was well-reasoned and does not warrant interference.

cases.case_name: Gian Singh v. State of Punjab
cases.principle: Regarding the power of the High Court under Section 482 CrPC to quash criminal proceedings for non-compoundable offences on the basis of a settlement agreement between the parties, particularly where the dispute is primarily private in nature.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The inherent jurisdiction of the High Court under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure should not be exercised to quash criminal proceedings involving serious, non-compoundable offenses on the basis of a settlement agreement, especially when the informant or injured victim is not a party to that agreement and has objected to it.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court's considered opinion was that the High Court certainly erred by quashing the FIR and the criminal proceedings on the basis of the Settlement Agreement, because the High Court failed to notice that the Appellant, who was an injured victim and the original complainant, was not a party to the Settlement Agreement and was not agreeable to such a course of action.
legal_tests_applied: In exercising its power under Section 482 CrPC to quash criminal proceedings based on a settlement, the High Court must consider whether it would be unfair or contrary to the interest of justice to continue with the criminal proceeding, or if continuation would tantamount to abuse of process of law despite the settlement, and whether to secure the ends of justice, it is appropriate that the criminal case is put to an end. (Gian Singh v. State of Punjab)
why_respondent_won: The High Court failed to notice that the Appellant, who was an injured victim and the original complainant, was not a party to the Settlement Agreement.
The Appellant was not agreeable to the course of action of quashing the proceedings based on the settlement.
The High Court's order neither secured the ends of justice nor prevented an abuse of the process of law, making it erroneous and contrary to the principles laid down in Gian Singh v. State of Punjab.
policy_considerations: The inherent power of the High Court under Section 482 CrPC must be exercised to secure the ends of justice or to prevent the abuse of the process of any court.

It is contrary to the interest of justice to continue with a criminal proceeding if a full and complete settlement between the victim and wrongdoer makes the possibility of conviction remote and bleak, but this principle does not apply when a key victim and the original complainant has not settled the matter.
